cards.explanation: The answer is True. Paul says his team has wronged no one. He says, "We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have exploited no one." Three "no one"s in a row, friends. That's a man reading off a clean list, and he says it while asking for room in their hearts (2 Corinthians 7:2).

The answer is that they're so close they live and die together. Paul says, "…you so occupy our hearts that we live and die together with you." That's not a casual friendship, friends. That's moving-in-and-staying closeness. And he says it right after making clear he isn't condemning them (2 Corinthians 7:3).

The answer is False. Paul says, "in all our troubles my joy overflows." The troubles are real, and the joy is bigger. His confidence and pride are great, and he says he's filled with encouragement too. His joy doesn't run dry (2 Corinthians 7:4).

The answer is conflicts outside and fears within. Paul says they were pressed from every direction, with "…conflicts on the outside, fears within." Trouble was coming at them from both sides. I think that's about the most tiring way to be squeezed. And it sets up what comes next (2 Corinthians 7:5).

The answer is Titus. Paul writes that "…God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus…" (2 Corinthians 7:6). Titus worked alongside Paul (2 Corinthians 8:23). Notice who gets the credit, friends. God is the one doing the comforting, and Titus is how it arrived.

The answer is their longing and zeal for Paul. Paul says Titus "…told us about your longing, your mourning, and your zeal for me…" Good news, delivered in person. Notice the zeal is for Paul, friends. That's why he says he rejoiced all the more (2 Corinthians 7:7).

The answer is rejoiced. Paul says Titus told them about the Corinthians' longing, mourning and zeal, "…so that I rejoiced all the more." All the more, friends. He was already comforted, and then the joy kept growing. That's a batch that comes out of the oven bigger than it went in (2 Corinthians 7:7).

The answer is that he does not regret it. Paul writes, "Even if I caused you sorrow by my letter, I do not regret it." He owns that it hurt. He doesn't pretend it didn't. And he stands by sending it (2 Corinthians 7:8).

The answer is that their sorrow led them to repentance. Paul says, "…I rejoice, not because you were made sorrowful, but because your sorrow led you to repentance." His joy isn't in the sorrow, friends. It's in where the sorrow led. That's a good father's heart (2 Corinthians 7:9).
The answer is False. Paul says they "…were not harmed in any way by us." Sorrow happened, but harm didn't. That's the sorrow God had intended. Paul puts it plainly (2 Corinthians 7:9).

The answer is salvation. Paul says, "Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret…" Salvation, friends, and nothing to regret afterward. That's the end of the road for this kind of sorrow (2 Corinthians 7:10).

The answer is death. Paul says, "…but worldly sorrow brings death." It's a heavy line, and he doesn't soften it. He sets it next to godly sorrow, which leads to salvation. Two kinds of sorrow, two very different endings (2 Corinthians 7:10).

The answer is innocent. Paul says, "In every way you have proved yourselves to be innocent in this matter." In every way, friends. That's right after his big list of what their godly sorrow produced (2 Corinthians 7:11).

The answer is so they'd see how devoted they were to him. Paul says he wrote "…that your earnestness on our behalf would be made clear to you in the sight of God." He says it was not on account of the one who did wrong or the one who was harmed. He wanted them to see their own earnestness. I think that's a gift, friends (2 Corinthians 7:12).

The answer is True. Paul says, "…we were even more delighted by the joy of Titus." He was encouraged already, and seeing Titus so happy topped it. His joy had a second helping. I'd take that every time (2 Corinthians 7:13).

The answer is False. Paul writes, "Indeed, I was not embarrassed by anything I had boasted to him about you." He also says "…our boasting to Titus has proved to be true as well." That's a relief if you've ever bragged on somebody ahead of time (2 Corinthians 7:14).

The answer is all obedient with fear and trembling. Paul says Titus remembers "…you were all obedient as you welcomed him with fear and trembling." All of them, friends, not just a few. That memory made Titus's affection for them even greater (2 Corinthians 7:15).

The answer is complete. Paul ends with, "I rejoice that I can have complete confidence in you." Complete, friends, with no gaps. After all that sorrow and repentance, it's a warm way to close (2 Corinthians 7:16).
